title: Ruxolitinib Rescues Multiorgan Clinical Autoimmunity in Patients with APS-1
abstract: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type-1 (APS-1) is caused by mono- or biallelic loss-of-function variants of the autoimmune regulator gene AIRE underlying early-onset multiorgan autoimmunity and the production of neutralizing autoantibodies against cytokines, accounting for mucosal candidiasis and viral diseases. Medical intervention is essential to prevent or attenuate autoimmune manifestations. Ruxolitinib is a JAK inhibitor approved for use in several autoimmune conditions. It is also used off-label to treat autoimmune manifestations of a growing range of inborn errors of immunity. We treated three APS-1 patients with ruxolitinib and followed them for at least 30 months. Tolerance was excellent, with no medical or biological adverse events. All three patients had remarkably positive responses to ruxolitinib for alopecia, nail dystrophy, keratitis, mucosal candidiasis, steroid-dependent autoimmune hepatitis, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, renal potassium wasting, hypoparathyroidism, and diabetes insipidus. JAK inhibitors were therefore considered an effective treatment in three patients with APS-1. Our observations suggest that JAK/STAT pathways are involved in the pathogenesis of APS-1 autoimmune manifestations. They also suggest that JAK inhibitors should be tested in a broader range of APS-1 patients.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Published in 2023 in the Journal of Clinical Immunology, this study has already accumulated 25 citations and sits in the top 10% most-cited papers for its field and year. Its influence is also visible in downstream reuse: the article has been reused or mentioned in 26 later works, including reviews, book chapters, preprints, and clinical articles focused on APS-1 and related autoimmune disease.

Full narrative

This article reports on ruxolitinib as a rescue therapy for multiorgan clinical autoimmunity in APS-1, a rare and severe disorder driven by AIRE loss-of-function and characterized by early-onset autoimmune complications. The paper’s impact has been especially strong within immunology and endocrine communities: the citing literature is concentrated in journals such as the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology and The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism, and the citation profile places the work in the top decile of its field-year cohort.

The scholarly record shows that the study is being used not just as a result to cite, but as a reference point for ongoing APS-1 work. Later articles have drawn on it in contexts ranging from diagnostic criteria and clinical management to broader discussions of inborn errors of immunity, while book chapters and review materials have incorporated it into synthesis pieces. That pattern suggests the paper has become part of the emerging clinical and translational framework around APS-1 and JAK inhibition.

The article’s reach is further supported by its reuse footprint and by scite, which records four mentioning citations. OpenAlex also shows a geographically and institutionally broad citing landscape, with strongest uptake in the United States and the United Kingdom and recurring presence from major research and healthcare institutions. This is consistent with a work that is moving from a specialized case-based report into a reusable clinical evidence point.

Support from NIAID and NCATS funding aligns with the translational character of the study, and the availability of open access through a hybrid model likely helped its early circulation. Public attention signals are quiet, so the record points primarily to academic and clinical uptake rather than broader media visibility. Overall, the article has already established clear scholarly traction for a rare-disease therapeutic approach with relevance beyond APS-1 itself.
